hints: Look closely at each amino acid and find the central alpha carbon (the CH). Which circled groups are attached directly to it, and which are out on the side chain R group?
Remember a peptide bond is always a condensation between an alpha amine and an alpha carboxyl to make -CONH-, so side chain groups 2 and 4 cannot be used.
walkthrough:
**Spot the alpha groups and the R groups**

Look for the central CH in each amino acid. That is the alpha carbon.

On the left amino acid, group 1 ($H_2N$-) is attached directly to the alpha carbon, so it is the alpha amine. Group 2 ($NH_2$) is at the end of a long side chain, so it is part of the R group. On the right amino acid, group 3 ($COOH$) is attached directly to the alpha carbon, so it is the alpha carboxyl. Group 4 ($COOH$) is at the end of the side chain, so it is part of the R group.

**Recall how a peptide bond forms**

A peptide bond is a condensation reaction between the alpha carboxyl group of one amino acid and the alpha amine group of another amino acid, with loss of water:
$$-COOH + H_2N- \rightarrow -CONH- + H_2O$$
The R groups are not involved. They stay free to give the amino acid its character.

**Pick the correct pair**

So we must join alpha to alpha. That is group 1 (alpha amine on the left) with group 3 (alpha carboxyl on the right). This matches option A.

options.A: Correct. Group 1 is the alpha amine and group 3 is the alpha carboxyl, and a peptide bond always forms between these two alpha groups.
options.B: Incorrect. Group 2 is an amine in the R side chain, not the alpha amine, and side chain groups do not form the peptide backbone.
options.C: Incorrect. Both 2 and 4 are R group side chain groups, so joining them would not make a standard peptide bond between the two backbones.
options.D: Incorrect. Although 1 is a correct alpha amine, 4 is the side chain carboxyl, not the alpha carboxyl, so this would be a side chain linkage.
